newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: PRESS DIGEST - NZ Business weeklies - Mar 21.
newsitem.headline: PRESS DIGEST - NZ Business weeklies - Mar 21.

text.p: In a flashback to its asset-stripping heyday, Brierley Investments is preparing to break up clothing and textile manufacturer LWR Industries and sell of its companies. The jewel in LWR's crown, sportswear-maker Canterbury International, is likely to be sold overseas. Buyers are already being sought. The rump of LWR will either be sold to "trade buyers" -- companies working in the manufacturing industry -- or be bought out by LWR management. Neither BIL nor LWR management will comment, but The Independent understands plans for the break-up are well advanced. Page 1.

The Consumers' Institute has called for an immediate cut to home mortgage interest rates as banks' profit margins hit a three-year high. Reserve Bank data show a sharp widening in the gap between floating mortgage rates and 90-day bank bill yields. "There's room to move and it's high time (banks) did," Consumer Institute chief executive David Russell said. Page 1.

Trustees of the Crown Forestry Rental Trust have doled out more than $12 million for research into Maori forestry claims. But they won't disclose to Finance Minister Bill Birch how the money is being used. Nor will they give details to the Federation of Maori Authorities. Birch, the federation and the Maori Council are responsible for appointing the trustees and the trust reports annually to them. Page 1.

Listener editor Jenny Wheeler announces her resignation from the weekly magazine today. When Wheeler took up the position just over two years ago she promised to lift circulation within two years or resign. Although her editorship has been marked by a notable rejuventation in the Wilson & Horton publication, circulation is erratic. In the ABC six monthly audit to December, circulation rose to 100,269 from 99,921. In the six months ending December 1995 circulation was 106,786. Page 3.

The Labour Party is about to re-brand itself in an attempt to stake out a clear identity in our increasingly cluttered political landscape. Branding has been the Beehive's buzz-word since MMP brought more parties into Parliament while reducting the differences between them. A main criticism of Labour has been that its lurch to the right in the 1980s, and factional infighting and weak communications since then, means no one understands what it stands for any more. page 3.

The government this week agreed to broker behind closed-doors talks between Clear and Telecom, and BellSouth and Telecom on the controversial issue of number portability -- or, more particularly, on how much one carrier should pay another when a customer decides to change his/her phone company. Several players in the industry -- Clear and BellSouth included -- are unhappy. They argue number portability is an issue affecting all New Zealand telecommunications companies and their customers, so talks should be neither bi-lateral, nor secret. Page 3.

The gloves are now officially off in the battle between two former trans-Tasman airline partners following the long-awaited sale of Qantas's 19.4 percent share of Air New Zealand's B shares. The shares were sold on Thursday to broker ANZ Securities for $425.6 million and distributed to a range of institutional investors in the United States, Asia, Britain, Australia and New Zealand. At $3.80 a share -- a discount of 15 cents on Thursday's closing sale price -- the sale earned Qantas a pre-tax profit of $110 million. Page 4.

Office products giant Blue Star has lost the Toshiba agency in Wellington for what Toshiba calls "a lack of performance." But Blue Star's Wellington regional manager Warren Sanders says the Toshiba agency was incompatible with its Sharp account and keeping Toshiba was not part of its long-term strategy. Instead, the Wellington Toshiba account has gone to Danka, which already holds it in Auckland. Page 4.

Public concern about potential conflicts of interest among those involved in Auckland's controversial $1.5 billion Britomart project has prompted the Auckland City Council to review its restraint of trade practices. Page 4

Sovereign Assurance this week launched a share option scheme for financial intermediaries and advisers selling its products. The scheme has a registered prospectus dated 14 March 1997. A first for any insurer in New Zealand, it will see participating brokers become eligible for Sovereign share option allocations. The number of options allocated depends on how many "qualifying points" brokers acumulate. These points, in turn, are tied to the volume and persistency of business written in any one of the three years ended 28 February 1998, 1999 or 2000. Page 6.

The ostrich investment company at the centre of a police fraud squad and Companies Office investigation was this week ordered to stop distributing its advertisements. The order has been made against Savannah Ostrich Processing Company by the Securities Commission. Page 6

Lion Nathan anticipates a drop in earnings following further slippage in the volume of beer sold in New Zealand in the last half-year. Company spokesman Graeme Seatter says the half-yearly earnings announcement on 28 April will reflect a two to three percent drop in beer sales, consistent with previous years. Seatter attributes the decline to changes in drinking habits, and government-sponsored anti-drink driving and moderation campaigns. Page 6. -- Wellington Newsroom (64 4) 4734746
